items.title: Monthly spending of a typical household
points: The pie chart shows how a typical household divides its monthly spending between six categories.
Housing is by far the largest expense, taking 32% of the budget, roughly a third.
Food comes second at 21%, followed by transport at 15%.
Leisure accounts for 12% and other items for 11%, while utilities are the smallest share at only 9%.
Overall, housing and food together make up more than half of all spending, at 53%.

items.title: Sources of electricity in one country, 2000 and 2020
points: The two pie charts compare the sources of electricity in one country in 2000 and 2020.
In 2000 coal was the dominant source at 45%, while wind and solar provided just 2%.
By 2020 coal had fallen sharply to 18%, and wind and solar had risen dramatically to 24%.
Natural gas grew from 25% to 32% and became the largest source, whereas nuclear and hydro stayed fairly stable, nuclear slipping from 15% to 14% and hydro edging up from 8% to 9%.
Overall, the country shifted away from coal towards gas and renewable energy over the twenty years.

items.title: Main reasons for visiting one city
points: The pie chart illustrates the main reasons why visitors travel to one city.
Holidays are the most common reason, accounting for 46% of visitors, almost half.
Visiting family is second at 22%, and business trips make up 18%.
Education represents 7%, while medical treatment is the least common reason at only 3%, with other reasons at 4%.
In short, the city attracts mainly leisure travellers, with personal and business visits well behind.

items.title: How university students spend their waking time on a weekday
points: The two pie charts compare how first-year and final-year students at a university spend their waking time on a typical weekday.
First-year students devote the largest share, 30%, to their social life, whereas final-year students spend the most time, 35%, on private study.
Private study more than doubles from 15% to 35%, while social life falls from 30% to 18% and lectures drop from 22% to 15%.
Sport is the smallest share in both groups, shrinking from 8% to 5%, and paid work rises slightly from 10% to 14%.
Overall, students become far more focused on independent study as they approach the end of their degree.

items.title: Composition of household waste in one city
points: The pie chart shows what household waste in one city is made up of.
Food waste is the largest component, at just over a third, 34%.
Paper and card make up 22%, and plastics account for 16%.
Glass represents 9%, while metals are the smallest category at only 5%, with other materials at 14%.
Overall, food and paper together form 56% of the waste, which suggests composting and paper recycling could reduce it significantly.

items.title: Land use in one region, 1980 and 2020
points: The two pie charts compare how land was used in one region in 1980 and 2020.
Farmland was the largest category in both years, although it declined from 48% to 41%.
The most striking change is urban land, which more than tripled from 6% to 19%.
Meanwhile, forest fell from 20% to 17%, grassland from 16% to 14%, and wetland more than halved from 7% to just 3%, the smallest share in 2020.
Overall, the region became much more urbanised at the expense of its natural and agricultural land.

items.title: Sources of research funding at a university
points: The pie chart illustrates where a university's research funding comes from.
Government grants are the main source, providing 41% of the total.
Industry contributes 23%, followed by charities at 14% and tuition fees at 10%.
The endowment supplies 7%, while other sources are the smallest share at 5%.
Overall, the university relies heavily on public money, although industry is also a significant partner.

items.title: How people travel to work in one city, 2005 and 2025
points: The two pie charts compare the ways people commuted to work in one city in 2005 and 2025.
The car was the most popular mode in both years, but its share fell considerably from 58% to 39%.
Cycling saw the biggest increase, rising from just 4% to 15%, and train use almost doubled from 10% to 18%.
Walking grew modestly from 9% to 12%, while bus use dipped slightly from 16% to 14%, and other modes remained the smallest share at 3% and then 2%.
Overall, commuters moved away from cars towards trains, bicycles and walking over the twenty years.

items.title: Water use in a typical home
points: The pie chart shows how water is used in a typical home.
Showers and baths account for the largest share, at 34%.
Toilet flushing is the second biggest use at 26%, followed by laundry at 14% and kitchen taps at 12%.
The garden uses 9%, while other purposes make up the smallest share at just 5%.
Overall, bathing and toilets together consume 60% of household water, so savings there would have the greatest effect.

items.title: Causes of land degradation in two types of region
points: The two pie charts compare the causes of land degradation in a dry region and a tropical region.
In the dry region overgrazing is the leading cause at 38%, whereas in the tropical region deforestation dominates at 41%.
Deforestation accounts for only 12% in the dry region, and overgrazing for just 14% in the tropical one.
Farming methods are important in both, at 30% and 25%, while mining is among the smallest causes at 5% and 6%.
Overall, the main threat to land depends heavily on climate: livestock in dry areas and tree clearance in tropical ones.
